title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
1. Ranking
Question: Which primary contributory causes appear most often?

Place primary_contributory_cause on Rows.
Place the row count measure on Text.
Sort descending by the count.
Exclude missing and not-applicable values.
Apply a Top 10 filter.

Check: The values should be integer record counts. If Tableau displays SUM(Number of Records), that is the count of rows at the current grain.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
2. Nominal comparison
Question: How does average injury count compare across the selected causes?

Keep the same selected causes from the ranking view.
Place primary_contributory_cause on Rows.
Place injuries_total on Columns.
Change the measure aggregation to Average.
Use bars and sort by the average.

Check: The axis should say average injuries per crash, not total injuries. Because most crashes have no reported injury, also inspect the distribution and the number of crashes in each group.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
3. Time series
Question: How does crash count change over time?

Confirm that crash_datetime is a recognized date/time field.
Place crash_datetime on Columns and choose a chronological month or year-month level.
Place the row count on Rows.
Use line marks and filter the date range if the full view is too dense.

Check: Determine whether the date pill is discrete or continuous. A continuous date creates a time axis; a discrete date creates headers. Do not connect unrelated categories with a line.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
4. Part-to-whole comparison
Question: Within each time period, what share of crashes falls in each most-severe-injury category?

Place time_period and most_severe_injury on Columns.
Place the row count on Rows.
Place most_severe_injury on Color.
Apply a Percent of Total table calculation if percentages are required.
Set the calculation direction so the percentages total 100% within each time period.

Check: Add the percentages for one time period. If they do not total approximately 100%, the table calculation is addressing the wrong direction or partition.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
5. Scatterplot
Question: How are observed temperature and dew point related?

Place temperature_f on Columns.
Place dew_point_f on Rows.
Place weather_station_name on Color or Filter.
Add crash_record_id to Detail, or turn off aggregate measures, so a mark represents a crash rather than one overall average.
Use transparency or a narrower date filter if overplotting hides the pattern.

Check: Many crashes can share the same hourly airport observation. A dense cluster does not mean each crash received an independent weather measurement. If the view contains only one or two marks, Tableau is aggregating the data.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
6. Distribution
Question: How does visibility differ across reported weather conditions?

Filter reported_weather_condition to several meaningful categories.
Place reported_weather_condition on Rows.
Place visibility_miles on Columns.
Add a box plot from the Analytics pane or Show Me, or create separate histograms using consistent bins.
Keep individual marks visible when useful for seeing unusual values.

Check: Compare medians, IQRs, and overlap. The officer-reported condition and airport observation are related but distinct measures; neither is a direct measurement at the exact crash location.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
7. Map
Question: Where are crashes in the selected analytical subset located?

Assign longitude to Columns and latitude to Rows.
Use a map or circle mark.
Add crash_record_id to Detail so separate crashes remain separate marks.
Place a meaningful category on Color only if it supports the question.
Filter to a manageable date, cause, injury, or geographic subset.

Check: Latitude belongs on Rows and longitude on Columns. Explain what the filter removes; a filtered map does not show the distribution of all crashes.

title: Lab 3 Hints
text:
Final quality check

Give every sheet a question-based title.
Include units in axes and tooltips.
Confirm every aggregation: count, sum, average, or percentage.
Verify filters apply to the intended worksheets.
Use consistent colors for the same categories across views.
Avoid interpreting unavailable or missing values as a known outcome.
Test at least one tooltip against the source row.

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
A survey estimate will rarely match the population exactly. Some differences arise from random chance; others arise because the survey process systematically includes, excludes, measures, or influences particular people.
The useful question is not simply, “Is this survey biased?” Instead ask:

At what stage could error enter, in which direction might it move the result, and what evidence would help us assess it?

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
section: Sampling and assignment answer different questions
text:
Sampling and assignment answer different questions
Survey research is usually observational: researchers measure people without assigning them to treatments. Two different forms of randomization have different purposes.








Design feature
Primary purpose
What it can support when well executed




Random sampling from a defined population
Make the sample resemble the population in expectation
Generalization to that population


Random assignment to conditions
Make treatment groups comparable in expectation
Causal conclusions about the assigned treatment



A random sample does not turn an observational relationship into a causal effect. Random assignment does not automatically make the participants representative of everyone else.






WarningTwo separate claims



Generalizability: Do the observed respondents represent the target population?
Causality: Does the study design rule out plausible alternative explanations for an observed effect?

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
Random sampling error
Different random samples from the same population produce different estimates. That chance variation is random sampling error.
Larger probability samples generally reduce random sampling error. Standard errors, confidence intervals, and margins of error describe this uncertainty when the sampling design supports those calculations.
Random sampling error does not consistently push estimates high or low. Increasing sample size can reduce it, but a very large biased sample can still be confidently wrong.

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
Systematic error and bias
Bias is systematic error: some feature of the design or data-collection process tends to move estimates away from the population value.
Bias is not the same thing as:

personal prejudice;
an unusual observation;
a skewed distribution; or
ordinary random variation from one sample to another.

A distribution may be strongly skewed and still accurately describe its population. Conversely, a survey result may look smooth and precise while systematically missing part of the population.

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
Follow the survey pipeline
Bias can enter at several stages.








Stage
Question
Common risk




Target population
Who do we want to understand?
The population is vaguely or conveniently defined


Sampling frame
Who could actually be selected?
Coverage or sample-selection bias


Recruitment
Who is contacted and invited?
Contact differences, inaccessible modes


Participation
Who responds?
Unit nonresponse and self-selection


Questionnaire
What is asked and how?
Wording, order, recall, or response-option problems


Response
How do people answer?
Social desirability, acquiescence, interviewer or mode effects


Processing
How are responses handled?
Coding, weighting, cleaning, or transcription errors


Reporting
What is communicated?
Selective emphasis, missing uncertainty, or overgeneralization

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
Coverage and sample-selection bias
Coverage error occurs when the sampling frame does not adequately cover the target population. The risk becomes bias when the omitted or overrepresented people differ on an outcome that matters.
Examples:

Using property-tax records to study all residents can omit renters.
Surveying only current customers cannot directly describe people who considered the product and left.
Posting a public survey link on one social platform overrepresents people who use that platform and encounter the post.

Diagnostic: Compare the target population, the sampling frame, and the final sample. Which groups can never enter the sample? Which groups have very different probabilities of selection?
Possible mitigation: Improve the frame, recruit through multiple channels, use probability sampling when feasible, and document groups that remain uncovered.

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
Nonresponse and self-selection
These ideas are related but not identical.

Nonresponse occurs when selected sample members do not provide usable responses.
Self-selection occurs when willingness or ability to participate helps determine who enters the respondent group, especially in opt-in samples.
Nonresponse bias occurs only when response is related to the survey outcome after considering the adjustments used in analysis.

A low response rate raises concern, but it does not by itself measure the size or direction of nonresponse bias. Respondents and nonrespondents must differ in a way that matters for the estimate.
Customer-satisfaction surveys illustrate the risk: customers with especially good or bad experiences may be more motivated to respond than customers with routine experiences.
Possible mitigation: Make participation accessible, reduce respondent burden, use reminders and appropriate incentives, compare respondents with known population benchmarks, and apply transparent weighting when justified.

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
Response and measurement bias
After agreeing to participate, respondents can still provide systematically distorted measurements.

Social desirability
People may report what seems acceptable rather than what is true, especially for sensitive behaviors, status, health, money, or ethics.


Acquiescence
Some respondents tend to agree with statements regardless of content. A page filled with similarly worded agree/disagree items can amplify this tendency.


Recall error
People may not accurately remember frequency, timing, or amount. “How many purchases did you make last year?” demands more memory than a shorter, clearly bounded period.


Mode and interviewer effects
Answers can differ across online, telephone, text, or in-person administration. An interviewer, perceived anonymity, device, or visual layout may change what people report.


Question wording and options
Leading, loaded, double-barreled, ambiguous, or assumption-based questions create measurement error. Response options that overlap or omit plausible answers force poor measurements.
Possible mitigation: Use neutral language, ask one idea at a time, provide exhaustive and mutually exclusive choices, permit “don’t know” or “prefer not to answer” when appropriate, pretest the questionnaire, and disclose the survey mode.

title: Bias and Error in Survey Research
text:
A practical example
Suppose ECO 230 students send an online campus-dining survey through their own social networks.

Coverage risk: Students outside those networks have no realistic chance to see the survey.
Self-selection risk: Students with strong dining opinions may be more likely to participate.
Measurement risk: A question such as “How dissatisfied are you with overpriced campus food?” assumes dissatisfaction and uses loaded language.
Reporting risk: Calling the respondents “UWL students” implies population coverage the design did not provide.

A more defensible report would describe the respondents and recruitment method, avoid a population-wide claim, show counts with percentages, and identify what a stronger sampling plan would require.

A data project is useful when it helps a stakeholder make a decision. A broad concern such as “traffic safety is getting worse” may motivate the work, but it is not yet an analysis question.
Use this chain:

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
A framing worksheet
Answer these questions before writing code:

What symptom, opportunity, or decision created the request?
Who will use the result, and what can that person or organization change?
What population, geography, and time period are in scope?
What outcome matters, and how is it represented in the data?
What explanatory or segmentation variables are available?
What resources, deadlines, and ethical constraints limit the project?
What related work or prior evidence should inform the analysis?
What would count as an actionable result?







TipA useful scope test



A strong question is simultaneously interesting, actionable, and answerable with the available data. Anything outside that overlap belongs in a limitation or a future-data recommendation.

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
Example: traffic crashes
Too broad: Why do crashes happen?
Better decision frame: A transportation safety team must decide which conditions and locations deserve targeted investigation.
Focused question: Among reported Chicago crashes from 2018 through 2025, which combinations of roadway conditions, weather, location, and time are associated with severe outcomes?
Possible objectives:

Describe crash counts and severity rates by year, season, and time of day.
Compare severe-outcome percentages across selected roadway and weather conditions.
Identify geographic areas with unusually high severe-crash counts after considering traffic volume if a suitable denominator is available.
Recommend two conditions or locations for deeper investigation.

Boundary: Crash records can show reported associations. They do not by themselves prove that a condition caused a crash or measure risk without an exposure denominator.

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
Example: short-term rentals
Too broad: What affects Airbnb prices?
Better decision frame: A tourism analyst wants to understand how the mix and pricing of listings differs across markets or neighborhoods.
Focused question: How do listed price and future availability differ by room type, capacity, and geography in the selected market snapshot?
Possible objectives:

Compare median listed price and IQR across room types.
Estimate how price changes with guest capacity while acknowledging other listing differences.
Describe the geographic distribution of listing types.
Identify segments that warrant a more detailed pricing analysis.

Boundary: Listed price is not necessarily the price paid. An unavailable calendar date is not necessarily a booked stay.

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
Example: appointments and satisfaction
Too broad: How can the clinic improve?
Better decision frame: A clinic manager needs to decide where a limited scheduling-improvement effort should begin.
Focused question: Which appointment characteristics are associated with no-shows, and how do satisfaction measures differ across operational segments in the synthetic, de-identified EHR data?
Possible objectives:

Measure no-show rates by appointment type, lead time, and time of day.
Compare satisfaction distributions across selected service groups.
Identify segments with both operational volume and unfavorable outcomes.
Recommend a pilot intervention and state what would be measured after implementation.

Boundary: The course EHR data supports analysis practice, not clinical decisions. Associations must not be interpreted as patient blame or medical causation.

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
Use specific objective verbs
Prefer verbs that make the expected result visible.



Purpose
Useful verbs




Summarize
Describe, measure, estimate, categorize


Compare
Compare, rank, assess


Explore relationships
Identify, examine, explore


Anticipate
Forecast, predict


Support action
Recommend, prioritize



Avoid using only “analyze” or “understand.” Those words do not tell the reader what evidence you will produce.

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
Turn expectations into hypotheses
A hypothesis is a specific, testable expectation. It should name variables and a direction or benchmark when a defensible direction exists.

Relationship

Listings that accommodate more guests tend to have higher listed prices.



Difference between groups

The severe-crash percentage differs between daylight and darkness conditions.



Comparison with a benchmark

The no-show rate for appointments scheduled more than 30 days in advance exceeds the overall no-show rate.

These hypotheses concern variables. “Chicago will differ from Milwaukee” is incomplete until you say which measured outcome will differ and how.

title: Problem Definition Examples
text:
Check the finished problem statement

Is the stakeholder named?
Is the decision or action clear?
Are the population, time, and geography bounded?
Is the outcome measurable with the available data?
Do the objectives collectively answer the question?
Are causal words avoided unless the design supports causality?
Are privacy, missingness, selection, and measurement risks acknowledged?

Percentage change
Percentage change compares a change with its starting value:
[ = ]











Comparison

title: Working with Percentages
section: Percentage points are not percent change
text:
Percentage points are not percent change
Suppose a response rate rises from 40% to 50%.

It increased by 10 percentage points: (50% - 40%).
It increased by 25% relative to the old rate: ((50 - 40) / 40 ).

These statements are both correct, but they answer different questions.

title: Working with Percentages
text:
Common denominator mistakes

Comparing counts when group sizes differ.
Dividing by the new value instead of the starting value for percentage change.
Ignoring missing values that shrink the denominator.
Mixing row and column percentages in one interpretation.
Reporting a large percentage change from a very small starting value without giving the counts.







TipReport counts and percentages together



Write “18 of 60 listings (30%)” rather than only “30%.” The count reveals the scale and makes the denominator auditable.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Descriptive statistics organize and summarize observed data. They help an analyst describe what is typical, how much observations vary, how categories are distributed, and whether variables appear to move together.
A summary does not automatically generalize beyond the data that were observed, and an association does not establish causation.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Descriptive statistics organize and summarize observed data. They help an analyst describe what is typical, how much observations vary, how categories are distributed, and whether variables appear to move together.
A summary does not automatically generalize beyond the data that were observed, and an association does not establish causation.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Measures of center

Mean: the arithmetic average. It is useful for quantitative data but can be pulled toward unusually high or low values.
Median: the middle ordered value. It is useful for ordinal or quantitative data and is resistant to extreme values.
Mode: the most frequent value or category. It is available for categorical data but may not be unique.

Choose the measure based on the variable’s meaning and distribution, not merely on which calculation is available in the software.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Frequency and grouped-summary tables

A frequency table reports counts for the categories of one variable.
A relative-frequency table adds percentages or proportions.
A cross-tabulation reports combinations of two categorical variables.
A grouped-summary table combines a categorical grouping variable with a quantitative measure, such as median listing price by room type.

For every percentage, name the denominator. Row, column, and table percentages answer different questions.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Measures of spread

Minimum and maximum: the observed endpoints.
Range: maximum minus minimum.
Interquartile range (IQR): the width of the middle 50% of observations.
Standard deviation: typical distance from the mean, expressed in the variable’s original units.

The median and IQR are often useful for skewed or outlier-prone data. The mean and standard deviation are most informative when the distribution is reasonably symmetric and unusual values have been investigated.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Measures of association
A cross-tabulation can reveal association between categorical variables. Correlation summarizes the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables on a scale from -1 to +1. Regression can describe how an outcome changes with one or more explanatory variables.
None of these methods proves that one variable caused another to change.

title: Data Sources
Data Sources
Data Sources
text:
Structured and unstructured data
Structured data are organized into defined fields, commonly rows and columns in a spreadsheet, database table, or Parquet file. Unstructured data include free text, images, audio, video, email, and other content without a single tabular schema.
ECO 230 primarily uses structured data. Some course datasets are large, messy, or assembled from several tables, but size alone does not make data unstructured.

title: Data Sources
text:
Questions to ask before analysis

Who created the data, and for what original purpose?
What does one row represent?
Which people, places, events, or time periods are included or excluded?
How were variables defined and measured?
What transformations occurred before you received the file?
Are there privacy, licensing, or redistribution restrictions?

title: Data Literacy Terminology
text:
Unit of analysis: the kind of entity or event being studied, such as a customer, transaction, listing, crash, patient encounter, or survey response.
Grain: the precise meaning of one row, including entity, event, time period, and any filtering conditions.
Observation: one row in a dataset.
Variable: an attribute or measurement recorded in a column.
Value: the entry for one variable in one observation.
Identifier: a label used to distinguish or join entities. An identifier may contain digits without being a meaningful numeric measure.







ImportantStart with the row



Before calculating a statistic, complete this sentence: One row represents one _____ for one _____ during one _____.

title: Data Literacy Terminology
text:
Variable roles and measurement scales








Scale
Meaning
Useful summaries




Nominal
Categories with no natural order
Counts, percentages, mode


Binary
A nominal variable with two categories
Counts, percentages, proportions


Ordinal
Categories with a meaningful order but unknown or unequal spacing
Counts, percentages, median, ordered displays


Interval
Numeric values with meaningful differences but no meaningful zero
Mean, median, range, IQR, standard deviation


Ratio
Numeric values with meaningful differences and a meaningful zero
Mean, median, range, IQR, standard deviation, ratios



A variable’s storage type in software is not necessarily its analytical role. For example, a ZIP code may be stored as a number but should be treated as a geographic identifier, not averaged.

title: Data Literacy Terminology
text:
Time variables

A duration, such as minutes required to complete a task, is quantitative.
A date or timestamp can be sorted, filtered, or used to calculate elapsed time.
A calendar category, such as month, quarter, or day of the week, is often used to group observations and must retain its natural order.
A year can represent time in a trend or act as a grouping category. Its treatment depends on the question.

For worked examples using current course data, see Understanding Data.

Independent Samples t-Test idt()




Steps 1-3: Setup

Test: Independent Samples t-test
Function: idt()

α = 0.05



Run the Test

h3 <- df %>%

h3$results

Paired Samples t-Test pst()




Steps 1-3: Setup

Test: Paired Samples t-test
Function: pst()

H0: \(\mu\)Black = \(\mu\)Green
HA: \(\mu\)Black \(\neq\) \(\mu\)Green
α = 0.05



Run the Test

h4 <- df %>%
  pst(~black_tea,~green_tea)







Step 4: Do we believe it?
h4$results
t(11) = -2.473, p = 0.031, r = 0.598, bf10 = 2.401

Decision Rule:

If p \(\leq \alpha\) → Reject H0

If p > \(\alpha\) → Fail to Reject H0




Decision:
p = 0.031 < 0.05 → Reject H0

Compare means for 2 independent groups
1 quantitative outcome; 1 categorical variable with 2 independent groups
Independent-samples t-test: idt(y ~ group)
\(H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B\)



Compare paired means
1 quantitative outcome measured twice or in matched pairs
Paired-samples t-test: pst(~ before, ~ after)
\(H_0: \mu_D = 0\)



Compare distributions or medians for 2 independent groups
Quantitative or ordinal outcome; 2 independent groups; mean is inappropriate
Wilcoxon rank-sum test: idw(y ~ group)
\(H_0\): The population distributions are equal.



Compare paired distributions or median differences
Quantitative or ordinal paired measurements
Wilcoxon signed-rank test: psw(~ before, ~ after)
\(H_0\): The population distribution of paired differences is centered at 0.



Compare means across more than 2 groups
1 quantitative outcome; 1 categorical variable with more than 2 groups
One-way ANOVA: ano(y ~ group)
\(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k\)



Compare one mean with a benchmark
1 quantitative variable and benchmark \(\mu_0\)
One-sample t-test: ost(~ y, mu = mu_0)
\(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\)

Hypothesis 1 - My Interpretation Steps 1-5

What statistical story am I attempting to tell?
Properties with a real bed listed will have higher list prices than properties with other bed types
What have I estimated or plotted to go along with that story and what is my conclusion from those estimates alone? If there was no uncertainty in these estimates, what should the business do?



Avg List Price by bed type


Properties that list real beds have a higher mean price than those that do not.
Which test is appropriate and what is the null hypothesis?
Analysis of Variance ano()
\(H_0\): \(\mu\) Airbed = \(\mu\) Couch = \(\mu\) Futon = \(\mu\) PO-Sofa = \(\mu\) Real Bed
\(H_A\): \(\mu\) Airbed \(\neq\) \(\mu\) Couch \(\neq\) \(\mu\) Futon \(\neq\) \(\mu\) PO-Sofa \(\neq\) \(\mu\) Real Bed
\(\alpha\) = 0.05 (you can use this as the default value)

What is the statistical interpretation of the test result?
F(4,731.84) = 404.918, p = 0, w = 0.353, bf10 = 4227346503043881200860804248400406882442082028864648
p is less than 0.05 (\(\alpha\)) so we reject the null hypothesis. Mean list price differs by bed type. Post hoc analysis reveals significant differences betweent the following bed types:

Airbed - PO-Sofa
Airbed - Real Bed
Couch - PO-Sofa
Couch - Real Bed
Futon - PO-Sofa
Futon - Real Bed
PO-Sofa - Real Bed

What is the practical interpretation of this analysis for a business audience? Are my estimates precise enough to tell the story I outlined in part (2)?
There is a significant difference in price based on bed type. Real bed had the highest mean list price as it was significantly higher than any other category. This makes sense as nicer properties are less likely to have worse bed options and owners will charge a premium for them. There were also several significant differences between other bed types. Couch and Airbed had significantly higher mean list prices than Pull-out Sofa. Pull-out Sofa had significantly higher mean list prices than Futon. There were some strange results in the post-hocs. There is no significant difference between couches and futons nor between airbeds and couches or airbeds and futons. This could indicate that there is variation in the non-real bed categories. Providing a real bed clearly has a benefit in terms of the list price, but there is not a conclusive advantage in one remaining category over the others. The effect size for this relationship is 0.36 which represents a large effect so this decision is not trivial. The Bayes factor is very large (> 100k) so there is decisive evidence for this effect. The effect is large and well supported with strong evidence that group differences explain a large share of the differences in price. It is likely that the choice of bed type will have a material impact on the list price so if a real bed is an option it should be listed.

What statistical story am I attempting to tell?

It is more likely for a property to have a strict cancellation_policy than any other cancellation_policy.

What have I estimated or plotted to go along with that story and what is my conclusion from those estimates alone?




X2 Goodness of Fit


Note: There are very few records in the super strict policies so we will have to filter them out.

Which test is appropriate and what is the null hypothesis?

Test Type: Chi Squared (\(X^2\)) Goodness of Fit Test csf()
\(H_0\): Cancellation_policy fits the Expected Model (default all categories equal)
\(H_A\): Cancellation_policy does not fit the Expected Model (default all categories equal)
\(\alpha = 0.05\)

h1 <- df %>%
  filter(cancellation_policy %in% c('flexible','moderate','strict')) %>%
  csf(~cancellation_policy)

print(h1)

Statistical Interpretation

X2(2) = 182.008, p = 0
p is less than 0.05 so we reject the null hypothesis. Cancellation_policy does not fit the expected model.

Practical Interpretation

Standardized residuals over 2 represent statistical significance so this effect is most likely not happening by chance.
Airbnb properties are much more likely to have a strict cancellation policy, likely to ensure operators generate income even if customers cancel reservations.
If you wanted to make your property stand out you might pick a moderate or flexible cancellation policy as they appear less common. However this comes with risk because cancellations become more likely.
Standardized residuals:

Freq

Cohen’s w indicates a small effect size so the overall effect of this relationship may be small. Strict policies appeared more often than expected, but the difference is not extremely high relative to the full distribution of cancellation policies. On the other hand, Bayes factor is extremely large indicating decisive evidence for the explanation that owners are much more likely to have a strict cancellation policy, it indicates that the decision is not random. This is likely representing a rather important real world effect, the increased risk of last minute cancellations may explain why those types of policies are used less freqently.

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
NotePurpose



This assignment helps you practice the Week 2 question:

How do we clearly describe the data we have?

You will build summary tables only (no charts yet) to describe:

Size (counts, missingness)
Center (mean or median)
Shape (spread: SD or IQR; optional percentiles)
Relationships (categorical ↔︎ categorical; continuous ↔︎ categorical)

You will also reflect briefly on how to use AI responsibly to accelerate—not replace—your thinking.

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
Objectives

Produce clean summary tables (no charts)
Choose statistics that match the measurement scale (NOIR)
Keep denominators straight (N, n_eligible, n_non-missing)
Describe relationships using group summaries and cross-tabs
Communicate results clearly with labels, units, and stated assumptions
Reflect on responsible AI use in data work

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
Resources

Week 2 slides (Size, Center, Shape, Relationships; Percentage Problems)
Week 1 slides (Unit of Analysis / Grain; Dimensions vs Measures; Tidy Data)
Dataset description files on Canvas







TipImportant



This assignment is graded for clear, careful completion.

No charts this week.
Your job is to be explicit and disciplined about what one row represents, what your denominators are, and which summaries are meaningful.

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
1) Choose Your Dataset (Week 1)

Select one of the four Week 1 datasets.
You may keep the same dataset from Homework 1 or switch.
In your submission, state:


Which dataset you used
Any filters or cleaning steps (e.g., removing blanks, focusing on a date range)

(No written response required beyond the brief notes above.)

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
2) Tools (You May Mix and Match)
Complete the tables using Excel, Tableau, posit.cloud, or any combination.

This does not all have to be in one tool.
Choose the tool(s) that best support the table you are trying to build.

(No written response required.)

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
3) Table 1 — Frequency Table (One Categorical Variable)
Create a frequency table for one categorical variable (≥ 3–4 categories recommended).
Your table must include:

Category
Count (n)
Percent of total
Any other information you feel is relevant.

Goal: Describe the distribution. What shows up a lot? What is rare?

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
section: 4) Table 2 — Continuous ↔︎ Categorical (Choose the Right Summary)
text:
4) Table 2 — Continuous ↔︎ Categorical (Choose the Right Summary)
Create a grouped summary table using:

One continuous measure (a numeric variable where arithmetic is meaningful)
One categorical dimension (≥ 3 categories)

Your table must include:

Group name
n_non-missing for the measure
A measure of center and/or measure of spread that matches your choice
Any other information you feel is relevant.

Below the table, write 1–2 sentences explaining why your choices are meaningful.

Tables 2–3 are intentionally flexible: your job is to decide what summary is most meaningful for your variables and explain why.

Hint from Week 2:

Mean/SD are most useful when the variable behaves like interval/ratio data with limited outliers.
Median/IQR are most useful when data are skewed, have outliers, or when “typical” is better captured by the middle.

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
section: 5) Table 3 — Another Continuous ↔︎ Categorical Relationship (Different Angle)
text:
5) Table 3 — Another Continuous ↔︎ Categorical Relationship (Different Angle)
Create a second grouped summary table, changing at least one of the following:

A different continuous measure, or
A different categorical grouping, or
A different summary choice (mean/SD vs median/IQR), or
A different filter or frame (e.g., weekday vs weekend, before vs after a date)

Requirements are the same as Table 2:

Group name
n_non-missing for the measure
A measure of center and/or measure of spread that matches your choice
Any other information you feel is relevant.

Goal: Answer a different question than Table 2.

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
6) Table 4 — Cross-Tab (Categorical ↔︎ Categorical) + Percentages
Create a cross-tab using two categorical variables, each with ≥ 3 categories.
Your table must include:

Cell counts
One percentage type (choose one and label it clearly):

Row % (conditional on row)
Column % (conditional on column)
Table % (overall share)

Row and column totals (margins)

Below the table, write one sentence that states the denominator clearly:

“These percentages are calculated as ________, so each ______ totals to 100%.”

Remember from Week 2:

Similar-sounding percentages can answer different questions. Make the numerator and denominator explicit.

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
(Optional) Continuous ↔︎ Continuous (Correlation Table)
If your dataset includes two continuous variables that might be related, you may include one small correlation table.
This is not required, but it is a strong way to explore whether two measures move together.
If you choose to include it, report:

n_non-missing (pairs)
Correlation r
1 sentence interpretation (direction + strength)

(Still no charts.)

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
text:
7) Findings Summary (Required)
Write 3 key takeaways (about 5–10 sentences total).
Each takeaway must:

Reference a specific table and at least one number (value + category)
Interpret what it implies (not just restate a statistic)

Strong examples:

“Group A has a higher median than Group B (Table 2), suggesting…”
“Under row %, Category X is concentrated in Y (Table 4), meaning…”
“Mean and median disagree (Table 3), which suggests skew/outliers…”

title: Homework 2: Exploratory Analysis
section: 8) Responsible Use of AI (Brief Reflection — Required)
text:
8) Responsible Use of AI (Brief Reflection — Required)
AI can help you move faster, but it must not make analytical decisions for you. Use AI only for clarification, rewriting, or troubleshooting.
Write 4–6 sentences responding to:
A. How did you use AI on this assignment? (If not at all, say so.)
B. What did AI help with (specific steps)?
C. What did AI miss, oversimplify, or get wrong?
D. Include one prompt you used and briefly note how it helped and where it fell short.
Remember our goal:

“Can you use AI responsibly to accelerate—not replace—your thinking?”

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
text:
Ethics is a relationship




People represented

Provide data, behavior, or experiences.



Analysts and researchers

Choose what to collect, combine, model, and report.



Decision makers

Act on the result and distribute its consequences.



Every analytical choice changes at least one of these relationships.

Connect “respondents” from the old deck to the broader category of people represented in administrative, transactional, sensor, and platform data.
[Sources] - Legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 2.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: Test the decision through six lenses
text:
Test the decision through six lenses








Lens
Ask




Purpose
What problem are we solving, and is this use necessary?


Permission
Would the people represented reasonably expect this use?


Privacy
What could be revealed, linked, or reidentified?


Fairness
Who benefits, who bears risk, and who could be excluded?


Transparency
Can we explain the data, method, limitations, and decision?


Accountability
Who can stop, correct, appeal, or repair a harmful outcome?




Use these six lenses for every scenario. Students should learn that an ethics review is a structured analysis, not a search for a magic yes/no rule.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: Who gets to reuse driving data?
text:
Who gets to reuse driving data?


CONNECTED VEHICLE DATA

An automaker records speed, braking, acceleration, and other driving signals. An insurer offers to buy access so it can price policies and investigate disputed claims.

Should the automaker sell the data to the insurer?



Ask groups to identify the original purpose, the proposed secondary use, affected parties, and one condition that would change their decision.
[Sources] - Legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 4.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
text:
Secondary use changes the bargain




Potential value


better evidence about a claim;
pricing that reflects measured behavior;
incentives for safer driving; and
faster fraud investigation.



Potential harm


unexpected surveillance;
inaccurate or context-free signals;
higher prices without meaningful appeal; and
exposure of passengers or household members who never agreed.









Before deciding


Specify consent, data minimization, retention, validation, access controls, allowed uses, and an appeal process.





Emphasize that a plausible benefit does not erase governance requirements. Ask whether the same data should be available for claim investigation and routine pricing.
[Sources] - Scenario adapted from legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 4.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: Can a company reveal a pseudonymous user?
text:
Can a company reveal a pseudonymous user?


IDENTITY INFERENCE

A messaging user chooses a pseudonym. Other users have stored the person’s real name in their contacts, allowing the platform to infer the identity and attach additional demographic information.

Should the platform uncover and use the person’s real identity?



Ask whether a real-name clause in the terms of service resolves the ethical problem. Then ask what the user’s behavior communicates about their expectations.
[Sources] - Legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 5.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
text:
De-identified does not mean harmless

Direct identifiers removed

↓

Records linked with contacts, location, behavior, or public information

↓

A person or household may become recognizable again







Expectation gap


What a system can infer may exceed what a person believed they disclosed.





Separate pseudonymity from anonymity. Ask which combinations of otherwise ordinary fields could make a person recognizable.
[Sources] - Scenario adapted from legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 5.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
text:
Access does not create permission


CONFLICT OF INTEREST

An intern can edit automated risk tags used by colleges. The intern discovers unfavorable tags attached to a family member’s profile and has valid credentials to change them.

Should the intern alter the family member’s records?



The original scenario used a younger brother and named example tags. The replacement keeps the conflict but removes distracting details.
[Sources] - Legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 6.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: The ethical action fixes the system
text:
The ethical action fixes the system

The intern should not secretly alter one record.
Instead:

preserve the audit trail;
disclose the conflict of interest;
use the documented correction or appeal process;
test whether similar tags are inaccurate for other people; and
escalate a systemic problem rather than creating a private exception.








Access versus authority


Technical capability answers “Can I?” Governance answers “Am I authorized, accountable, and acting consistently?”





Connect this to database credentials, shared Posit projects, grading data, and any other environment where permission is broader than the legitimate purpose.
[Sources] - Scenario adapted from legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 6.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: A helpful model can still cause harm
text:
A helpful model can still cause harm


HEALTHCARE PAYMENT RISK

A healthcare organization predicts who may have trouble paying a bill. The score could connect patients with assistance, but it uses demographic and medical factors and may also affect access before services occur.

Should the organization use the model?



Do not let students answer only by pointing to good intentions. Ask them to distinguish a supportive intervention from a punitive one.
[Sources] - Legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 7.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: The same score can support or punish
text:
The same score can support or punish








Supportive use
Punitive use




Offer financial counseling
Delay or deny care


Simplify payment options
Increase scrutiny without explanation


Connect people with assistance
Use health information unrelated to ability to pay


Let staff review context
Treat the score as an unquestionable fact










The model is only part of the system


Evaluate the outcome, training data, error rates, affected groups, intervention, human review, and appeal process together.





Ask who experiences false positives and false negatives. A model can be statistically accurate overall and still create unacceptable consequences for a subgroup or use case.
[Sources] - Scenario adapted from legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 7.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
text:
Write an ethical decision record


Purpose: What decision or benefit justifies the analysis?
People: Who is represented, affected, excluded, or able to object?
Data: What was collected, inferred, joined, and retained?
Evidence: How well does the method work, and for whom?
Risks: What foreseeable misuse, error, or unequal consequence exists?
Controls: What consent, minimization, review, security, and appeal are required?
Decision: Proceed, redesign, restrict, or stop - and who owns that choice?


This converts the old closing checklist into a record that can be reviewed later. Point out that ethical analysis should be reproducible just like statistical analysis.
[Sources] - Expanded from legacy D14_Slides.pptx, slide 8.

title: Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
Week 14 - Ethics in Business Analytics
section: Can you defend the decision to the people affected?
text:
Can you defend the decision to the people affected?


Good analysis is not only accurate.
It is purposeful, proportionate, explainable, contestable, and accountable.


Return to the opening question. Ask students which lens changed their first reaction and why.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research

The goal








Good sample


A good sample is random enough to protect against selection bias and representative enough to reflect the population we care about.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
section: Randomness is not the same as representativeness
text:
Randomness is not the same as representativeness










Representative
Not representative




Random
Best case
Possible, especially with small samples or bad frames


Not random
Possible, but harder to defend
Common convenience-sample problem

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Random








Random sample


Every unit in the frame has a known chance of being selected.





Random sampling helps protect us from hidden selection rules.
It does not guarantee perfection in every single sample.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Representative








Representative sample


The sample resembles the population on variables that matter for the question.





Representative is about the result.
Random is about the process.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Random but not representative

This can happen when:

the sample is small
the frame is flawed
an important subgroup is rare
the random draw is unlucky
nonresponse changes the final data

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Nonrandom but representative

This can happen, but it usually requires careful control.
Examples:

quota sampling
judgment sampling
balanced recruitment
post-stratification or weighting








Tradeoff


Nonrandom samples can be useful, but they are harder to defend.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Same goal, different risks

Every sampling method is trying to answer:

How do we learn about the population without measuring everyone?


But each method creates different risks.

Probability Sampling

Non Probability Sampling

The important comparison








Not just the estimate


Two samples can have similar averages but very different subgroup composition.





Representation is about who is in the data, not just whether one number looks close.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Random Sampling Error








Random sampling error


Random sampling error is the difference caused by selecting one random sample instead of another.





It is noise from sampling.
It is not the same as bias.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
The transition








Measurement problem


Even if we sample the right people, we can still ask the wrong question.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Select One

Use select-one questions when respondents should choose one best answer.
Example:

What is your primary way of getting to campus?








Design check


Are the choices mutually exclusive enough for the question?

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Select All That Apply

Use all-that-apply when multiple answers can be true.
Example:

Which tools have you used for coursework this semester?








Interpretation warning


The percentages across choices usually do not add to 100%.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Likert Scale

Likert scales make attitudes easier to measure consistently.
Example:

I feel confident interpreting statistical results.


Strongly disagree -> Strongly agree

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Semantic Differential

Semantic differential scales measure perception between opposite ideas.
Example:

Statistics feels…


Easy 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Difficult

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Numeric Scales Need Anchors

Bad:

Rate your confidence from 0 to 100.


Better:

0 = not confident at all
50 = somewhat confident
100 = completely confident

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Constant Sum








Constant sum


Respondents allocate a fixed number of points across options.





Use it when you want prioritization.
Electronic surveys can enforce the total.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Graphic Rating Scales

Graphic scales can help when numbers or words are difficult.
Useful in:

child surveys
low literacy contexts
medical pain scales
fatigue or communication difficulty

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Drilldown Questions








Drilldown


Start broad, then narrow the choices.





Better than forcing people through a giant pick list.
Example:
College -> Department -> Major

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Leading Question

Bad:

How much do you agree that this helpful course improves your analytical thinking?


Problem:
The wording pushes respondents toward a positive answer.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Loaded Question

Bad:

How often do you waste time using AI instead of thinking for yourself?


Problem:
The wording judges the respondent before they answer.

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Double-Barreled Question

Bad:

The Shiny apps are easy to use and help me learn the material.


Problem:

title: Week 12 - Sampling and Survey Research
text:
Assumption Question

Bad:

How often do you use ChatGPT to complete your homework?


Problem:
It assumes the respondent uses ChatGPT.

text:

If yes, how often?
If yes, for which tasks?
What did you check yourself?


Use this to connect back to responsible AI expectations from earlier homework.

who could be selected

Before trusting a survey result


Ask: who was in the frame, how were they sampled, who responded, and how was the question worded?

Tells us nothing about importance because p depends on sample size

title: Week 7 - Testing Hypotheses
text:
Effect Sizes
Effect sizes describe the size of a relationship or difference.

How big is the effect?
Is the difference meaningful in practice?
How much of the outcome is explained?



Small


Medium


Large





Larger effect sizes mean a stronger relationship, bigger difference, or more explained variation.

Smaller effect sizes mean the pattern is weaker, even if it is statistically significant.











p-Value vs Effect Size


p-values answer “Is it statistically detectable?”, Effect sizes answer “Is it practically meaningful?”

title: Week 7 - Testing Hypotheses
text:
Mike’s Dumb Casino


What happened?

Before seeing the tens die
Chance of winning = 7%
After seeing 90 on the tens die
Chance of winning = 70%

What evidence strength causes this update?
Prior odds:
\[
\frac{0.07}{0.93} \approx 0.075
\]
Posterior odds:
\[
\frac{0.70}{0.30} \approx 2.33
\]
Evidence multiplier:
\[
BF_{10} \approx \frac{2.33}{0.075} \approx 31
\]


  

Seeing the tens die = 90 provides about 30:1 evidence for winning.

title: ECO 230
text:
This exercise is intended to help you prepare for the practical portion of your final exam. Please review the prompt carefully before you arrive in class. The scenario and data description are included here. You will receive the actual data at the start of class. This exercise is open note, book, Google etc, but is not a team exercise. You must complete your work in the classroom without communicating with others. However, you are welcome to discuss the prompt and your strategy with others before class. The rubric does include points for originality of work.






NoteScenario



The NCAA adopted an interim name, image, and likeness (NIL) policy in June 2021, and college athletes were allowed to begin receiving compensation for NIL activities on July 1, 2021. In practice, this means athletes may be paid for sponsorships, endorsements, social media promotions, appearances, merchandise, camps, and other uses of their personal brand.
Supporters argue that NIL gives athletes access to income and business opportunities connected to the value they help create. Critics worry that NIL may increase inequality between schools, blur the line between college and professional sports, and make recruiting more complicated. Either way, NIL has made some college athletes much more visible to the public than they would have been under the old rules.
You work for a consulting firm hired by a consortium of Division 1 universities to understand whether this new sports visibility matters for admissions. Your team is interested in whether attention around well-known athletes or successful sports programs is connected to student interest in the university.
Your team has been asked to answer two questions:

Does having a famous athlete increase university enrollment?
Does having a successful sports program increase university enrollment?

Your team has been compiling a database to address these questions for recent admission cycles. You only have two years of data collected so far, but you’d like to do some preliminary analysis.








NoteData Description



The data grouping is panel.
The unit of analysis is one observation per university for each year (2024 and 2025).
The variables are:

year: which contains values 2024 or 2025
applications: count of applications received by each school
top25: percentage of students in the incoming class who were ranked in the top 25% of their high school graduating class
verbal500: percentage of students in the incoming class with verbal SAT scores of 500 or greater
mth500: percentage of students in the incoming class with math SAT scores of 500 or greater
famous_athlete_lastyr: binary variable equal to 1 if the school had a nationally famous athlete with major NIL/media visibility in the prior year
bowl_lastyr: binary variable equal to 1 if the school made it to a bowl game in the prior year
finfour_lastyr: binary variable equal to 1 if the school’s men’s basketball team made the final four in the previous year
school: school name









NoteRequirements



Using Excel, Tableau and Posit.cloud, please conduct preliminary analysis of the questions above. Your analysis should include:

At least one graph
At least one table
At least one hypothesis test
A brief bullet point summary of your findings and limitations
Work in Posit.cloud and work in either/or Tableau, Excel

You do not need to address both questions. You may choose to focus on only one if you like.








NoteSubmitting Completed Work



Upload your Excel workbook, your Tableau Packaged Workbook, and your knit RMarkdown .pdf to Canvas.
After you upload your submission, you will be able to view other student submissions in the discussion thread.

title: ECO 230 Business and Economic Research & Communication
text:
Course description
Building on the foundation in statistics acquired in STAT 145, students will continue to develop and will apply skills in data analysis to aid in business decision making. These skills include data collection, data summarization, data visualization, statistical inference, and communication of data in business contexts. Students will learn and apply best practices for research design and analysis to address authentic business cases. Students will build these skills in collaboration with each other and through engagement with business and community leaders. The course also discusses effective survey design and current privacy and ethical issues in collecting and using data. Prerequisite: ENG 110 or ENG 112; STAT 145; CBA major, CASSH economics major, or healthcare analytics management minor. Offered Fall, Spring.

Prerequisites
Prerequisite: ENG 110 or ENG 112; STAT 145; CBA major, CLS economics major, or Healthcare Analytics Management Minor.

title: ECO 230 Business and Economic Research & Communication
text:
Learning outcomes

Mapped to CBA Undergraduate Curriculum Goals and Objectives

Develop the ability to articulate a business problem or opportunity using qualitative and quantitative evidence and propose an analysis plan to identify potential solutions, including collection of primary data via surveys. (CT-1)
Describe, summarize, and interpret data using descriptive statistics, inferential statistics, and data visualization.
Develop foundational skills related to spreadsheets, interactive data visualization software, and scripting languages used for data analysis and visualization.
Communicate the purpose, methods, and results of analysis to authentic audiences in appropriate written and oral formats. (CS-1, CS-2)
Apply research design and data analysis best practices to complete case-based projects and to critique others’ analyses. (CT-1)
Describe current debates in research ethics and data privacy and the implications for business research. (SR-1)



CBA Undergraduate Curriculum Goals and Objectives referenced above

Communication Goal: Our students will be able to convey information and ideas effectively.

(CS-1) Learning Objective: Students will convey information and ideas in professional business reports

(CS-2) Learning Objective: Students will convey information and ideas in oral presentations.

Decision Making and Critical Thinking Goal: Our students will be able to think critically when evaluating decisions.

(CT-1) Learning Objective: Students will evaluate alternatives and understand the ramifications of those alternatives within a given business context.

Social Responsibility Goal: Students will demonstrate the role of social responsibility in business decisions.

(SR-1) Learning Objective: Students will be able to identify and apply different frameworks of social responsibility to business problems and recognize the short- and long-term effects on stakeholders and society.


Remaining CBA Goals and Objectives along with rubrics for each can be found here:
https://www.uwlax.edu/cba/undergraduate-curriculum-learning-goals-and-objectives2/#tmcommunication-goals

Grading

Calculations
Your overall grade consists of the following assessments, arranged by type and value. Your final grade can be computed by multiplying the scores received by the percentages reported below to arrive at a weighted average. Team assignments are denoted by (T) but please note grades received for team project deliverables will be adjusted by your Peer Evaluation score.

Calculation of individual grades for team project work
All work for the assignments denoted as Team Projects by (T) above will be scored out of 100 points to assign a Team Grade. Individual grades will be computed by multiplying the Team Grade by the CATME peer evaluation score you receive for that work. The CATME peer evaluation is a psychometrically validated and behaviorally anchored rating scale developed under a National Science Foundation Grant and used by universities throughout the country. Through a secure web-based platform, you will rate your own and your teammate’s performance on each project. This information will be reported in the aggregate to your teammates (they cannot see who gave them what scores) and will produce a Peer Evaluation Score. Most students receive a score of 1, those that exhibit exceptional performance receive scores above 1 with a maximum of 1.05. Underperforming teammates receive scores below 1, and as low as 0.4.






Note



Note: This is not a “zero sum game”. It is possible for team members to get scores above 1 without others getting scores below. The algorithm flags evaluations that appear to manipulate ratings to inflate their own scores. Your score will automatically be reduced by 0.05 if you fail to complete the Peer Evaluation on or before the due date.




Grievance procedure for peer evaluation scores
Poor peer evaluations can lead an individual grade to fall substantially below the Team Grade. For example, a project that received a score of 95/100 would produce an individual grade of 38/100 if you receive a peer evaluation score of 0.4. If you feel the score you received does not accurately reflect your contributions to Team Project work, you have the option to file a grievance. To do so you must follow this procedure:

Within 2 business days of the official notification that grades have been posted, communicate to your instructor via email your intent to file a grievance. Official notifications of grade posting will appear on Canvas notifications.
Within 1 business day of notifying your intent, prepare and email a one page formal letter addressed to your teammates and including the following information:

Your understanding of the work you had agreed to do for the deliverable. Be sure to refer to any documentation that is relevant (Meeting Minutes, emails or group chats, revision histories in documents etc.). Be prepared to provide any documentation you mention in the letter if requested.
A summary of the work you actually did. Refer to documentation as above.
Justification for any discrepancies between (a) and (b). If this documentation includes any confidential health or personal matters you do not wish to disclose to your team, please raise this with me or contact Student Life Office for council. Note: In these cases it is best to reach out to me or Student Life before you are at the point of receiving a bad peer evaluation.
A statement of the peer evaluation score you believe you have earned.

If after reviewing your letter I believe the case has merit, I will send it on to your teammates and schedule an arbitration. If I determine no arbitration is warranted, I will schedule a one-on-one meeting with you to discuss.
If arbitration is warranted, it must be conducted in-person with all team members present. The only exception to this requirement would be a case where the timeline in the procedure would place the earliest possible arbitration date after the final exam date. In those cases, a virtual meeting may be agreed upon or incomplete grades may be assigned until an in-person meeting can be scheduled. I will serve as the arbitrator. You and your teammates will have the opportunity to present your case and reconcile evidence referenced in your letter. At the end of the meeting, all team members (including yourself) will submit the score they believe you have earned to me via secret ballot. I will use this information in making my final determination, but the final determination is mine alone.



Late assignments, missed quizzes

Individual assignments






Warning



Individual assignments are due on the dates indicated on the Canvas Weekly Agendas. Late or missing assignments will not be graded. All assignments in a module must be completed before the Module Quiz. If extenuating circumstances impact your ability to meet deadlines or participate in class activities, you are responsible for alerting me as soon as possible. When conflicts are known ahead of the deadline you must notify me ahead of the deadline. All communication regarding missed or late individual work should be confirmed by email - even if we speak in person or during student hours, you must follow up via email to confirm so that we both have a record of the agreement.




Team assignments
Deadlines for Team Assignments may be extended for the entire class if there are extenuating circumstances or granted to teams if requested with appropriate justification and all team members agree to the request. Presentations cannot be delayed unless there is a major emergency or complication. For other deliverables, extensions must be requested at least 1 business day before the due date. title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Earlier in the course, you analyzed data and communicated results.
For Project 2, we step back and ask a more fundamental question:
Why should we trust a result enough to act on it?
Your job is to identify a real problem, opportunity, or decision and design a study that could produce evidence people would actually believe.
You will not collect the data and you will not complete the final analysis.
Instead, you will design how the evidence should be produced and defend why that design is strong enough to matter.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Earlier in the course, you analyzed data and communicated results.
For Project 2, we step back and ask a more fundamental question:
Why should we trust a result enough to act on it?
Your job is to identify a real problem, opportunity, or decision and design a study that could produce evidence people would actually believe.
You will not collect the data and you will not complete the final analysis.
Instead, you will design how the evidence should be produced and defend why that design is strong enough to matter.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Core Goal
This project is about study design, not repeating hypothesis tests for their own sake.
Your proposal should make a clear case that:

the question matters
the design fits the question
the data would be collected in a credible way
the results would be trustworthy enough to inform a real decision

If you include research objectives or a tentative hypothesis, they should support the design rather than overshadow it.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Deliverables
You will complete the following:

Week 13 informal topic meeting
Week 14 informal presentation
Week 14 Red Team critique
Final written proposal before the final exam

The written proposal may take the form of an executive summary, outline, or combined proposal document, depending on the course materials used in class.

Before the Final

The final written proposal should incorporate the feedback you received during the Week 14 pitch, critique, and rebuttal discussion.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Topic Options
You may focus on:

a real business situation you know through work, family, or your personal network
an academic question connected to your major field of study
a case study or industry problem where you can propose a new research design
any topic you genuinely find interesting

Because you are not required to complete the project, you are encouraged to be ambitious. You are also not limited to methods we have practiced in class, but if you propose a more advanced method you are responsible for explaining why it fits the problem.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
In-Class Format
Project 2 will use a pitch-and-critique format.

Proposing Team
Your team will act like a group seeking support for a research idea.
Your job is to:

pitch the problem
explain the study design
defend why the design is credible



Red Team
Another team will act as your Red Team.
Their job is to challenge your proposal by identifying weaknesses such as:

sampling problems
design or measurement flaws
weak generalization or causal reasoning
ethical concerns



Audience
The rest of the class should think like skeptical decision-makers:
Would we trust this result enough to act on it?

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Suggested Pitch Structure
Your in-class pitch should briefly cover:

the problem or opportunity
the research question
the proposed design
why the evidence would be trustworthy
the biggest known risk

Your goal is not to prove the answer in advance.
Your goal is to convince the audience that your design is worth taking seriously.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Written Research Proposal Guidance
The written research proposal is the final product of this process.
In other words:

Week 13 is an informal topic discussion
Week 14 is the pitch, Red Team critique, and rebuttal
the final written research proposal should reflect what your team learned from that feedback

There is an Analysis Plan Outline in the Week 12 canvas materials. You do not need to fill it out as a form, but it may help you think through the elements your proposal should include.
A good target is about 2-4 pages in paragraph form.
The Analysis Plan Outline can still be useful as a guide or idea starter. The written research proposal rubric lines up with it roughly as follows:

Written Research Proposal 1: Problem / Opportunity -> mostly aligns with Outline Section 1
Written Research Proposal 2: Research Question and Direction -> mostly aligns with Outline Sections 2-4
Written Research Proposal 3: Study Design and Measures -> mostly aligns with Outline Section 5
Written Research Proposal 4: Trustworthiness, Risks, and Limits -> mostly aligns with Outline Sections 6 and 8

You do not need to follow the outline section-by-section or use those exact headings. The outline is there to help you think through what a strong final proposal should cover.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Required Components
The final written research proposal should clearly address the following components.

1. Problem or Opportunity
Explain the situation that motivates the project.
Your audience should understand:

what is happening
why it matters
who would use the results



2. Research Question
Your question should be:

specific
interesting
actionable

A strong question implies a real decision.


3. Proposed Study Design
You may propose a:

survey
observational study
experiment
predictive model
or another justified design

Explain clearly:

who or what is being studied
what information would be collected
how the data would be collected



4. Why Should We Trust It?
This is the heart of the assignment.
You must make a case for trustworthiness by addressing:
Population and Sampling

Who is represented?
Who might be missing?
How could the sample become misleading?

Measurement and Design

Are you measuring the right thing?
Are the variables or questions well designed?
What could go wrong in data collection?

Generalization or Causal Claims

If this is observational, what can and can you not conclude?
If this is experimental, what causal claim would be justified?
If this is predictive, why should it generalize to new cases?

Ethics

Who could be harmed?
Who could be excluded?
What privacy, fairness, or consent concerns matter here?



5. Known Risks and Limitations
Even if the project is well designed, how could it still fail?
Be specific. This is one of the most important parts of the assignment.


6. Optional Supporting Structure
If helpful, you may also include:

short research objectives
a tentative hypothesis or expected pattern
a high-level analysis plan

These can strengthen the proposal, but they are not the main focus. The central question is still whether the design would produce evidence worth trusting.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Grading
Project 2 will be graded across four parts:

Week 13 informal meeting: 10
Week 14 informal presentation: 10
Week 14 Red Team critique: 10
Written proposal 1 - Problem / Opportunity: 15
Written proposal 2 - Research Question and Direction: 15
Written proposal 3 - Study Design and Measures: 20
Written proposal 4 - Trustworthiness, Risks, and Limits: 20

Total: 100 points

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Grading Emphasis
Your work will be judged mainly on:

clarity and importance of the problem
quality of the research question
fit between the question and the design
quality of the trustworthiness reasoning
attention to bias, limitations, and ethics
clarity of oral and written communication

Students who identify honest weaknesses and explain them clearly will usually be stronger than students who pretend their design has none.

title: Project 2: Can We Trust It?
text:
Key Principle
Good analysis cannot rescue bad design.
If the design is weak, the result should not be trusted.
If the design is strong, the result becomes worth arguing about.

Prompt

PROMPT

title: GROUP PROJECT – DATA ANALYSIS PROJECT
text:
Resources






Note



RESOURCES








Warning



RECOMMENDATIONS FOR YOUR ANALYSIS



Decide what stories you will be working on as soon as possible. Your story may evolve over time, but having an idea of what information you are trying to get out of your data set will assist in cleaning up your data set, defining and testing your hypotheses and developing your presentation.
Have a discussion about how you want to divide work within your group. Are you each going to be working on one story, are some members going to specialize in data analysis while others specialize on developing the presentation.
The backbone of your analysis will be performed and documented in R. This will include cleaning your data set to prepare it for analysis. Descriptive and inferential statistics and, if you prefer, visualizations. You can export data and perform analysis in Excel/Tableau, but the data set you are using for analysis should be prepared in R. This not only makes it easier to document how your data was prepared, but also helps to ensure that everyone in your group is working with the same data set.
With the exception of the inferential statistics (which we will start using in Week 6) you have already performed some version of the analysis you are expected to do for this project in earlier assignments. This is the same type of work we have been doing so far in the class, just more of it. Feel free to recycle analysis that you did for previous assignments; if it supports your story or helps to address your hypothesis there is no need to start over from scratch.
Make good use of the multiple weeks you have to work on this project; you do not want to wait until the last minute.
Pick stories that you think are interesting. It will make your presentation more compelling if you are actually invested in the story you are telling. It will also make your analysis seem like less of a chore.







Warning



DATA


Full data sets are provided in the project templates per topic. Some of these data sets are quite large so a good early step is to filter out data that is not needed to address your hypotheses. It will make your analysis run faster and make the sizes of your files easier to deal with if you are doing analyses in Excel or Tableau. Some examples of common data cleaning tasks are included in your posit.cloud project; feel free to adapt them to your needs.

PRESENTATION MATERIALS


Your presentation may be prepared in either Google Slides or PowerPoint. If using PowerPoint, you are encouraged to use Office Online to enable all team members to access the presentation and contribute. Effective slide design will be covered in class, and the principles of effective design are reflected in the rubric included under Grading Criteria. All team members are responsible for the content of all slides and the presentation should be cohesive, even if you have delegated the design of certain sections to separate team members.






Warning



ORAL PRESENTATION


All teams will present their work in a formal business presentation. Ask your instructor about the presentation location, times, and venue (e.g., seated conference room style vs. standing). The following expectations apply to all sections:

No notecards

Dress is business casual or more formal

All team members must speak

The audience may interrupt to ask questions during the presentation. Plan for 8–10 minutes of content, not including questions.

Presentation content should be non-technical. Slides should not contain technical output of hypothesis tests and the oral delivery should not include detailed discussions of statistical tests. However, students should be prepared to answer technical questions if prompted and may choose to have supplemental content prepared at the end of the presentation materials in anticipation of technical questions.

DOCUMENTING YOUR ANALYSIS


All teams must create RScripts or RMarkdown documents containing sufficient annotations to enable an outside reader to understand and replicate their work. Code should be “tidy”, meaning code following each pipe in a dplyr call begins on a new line. For ease of dividing work across team members, you may prepare separate RScripts or RMarkdown documents for each piece of your analysis. If you choose to do this, provide a single document that lists the file name of each RScript or RMarkdown with a brief description of contents.
