Oral presentation rubric






Warning



ORAL PRESENTATION RUBRIC







Trait
Capstone (4)
Milestone (3)
Milestone (2)
Benchmark (1)
Insufficient (0)




Organization
Organizational pattern (specific introduction and conclusion, sequenced material within the body, and transitions) is clearly and consistently observable and makes the content of the presentation cohesive.
Organizational pattern (specific introduction and conclusion, sequenced material within the body, and transitions) is clearly and consistently observable within the presentation.
Organizational pattern (specific introduction and conclusion, sequenced material within the body, and transitions) is intermittently observable within the presentation.
Organizational pattern (specific introduction and conclusion, sequenced material within the body, and transitions) is not observable within the presentation.



Verbal Delivery
Speaker’s voice enhances the effectiveness of the presentation and pace of the presentation maintains the interest of the audience. Language in presentation is appropriate to audience.
Speaker’s voice is always audible and appropriately expressive and pace of the presentation maintains the interest of the audience. Language in presentation is appropriate to audience.
Speaker’s voice is generally audible with some expression and pace of the presentation is natural. Language in presentation is appropriate to audience.
Speaker’s voice is inaudible or lacks expression and pace of the presentation is halting or too fast to understand. Language in presentation is not appropriate to audience.



Physical Delivery
Delivery techniques (posture, gestures and eye contact) make the presentation compelling, and speaker appears polished and confident.
Delivery techniques (posture, gestures and eye contact) make the presentation interesting, and speaker appears comfortable.
Delivery techniques (posture, gestures and eye contact) make the presentation understandable, and speaker appears tentative.
Delivery techniques (posture, gestures and eye contact) detract from the understandability of the presentation, and speaker appears uncomfortable.



Content and Supporting Material
Supporting material (presentation content, slides, or handouts) is relevant, compelling and lends credibility to conclusions. Message is fully tailored to audience.
Supporting material (presentation content, slides, or handouts) is relevant and generally sufficient to support the ideas. Message is tailored to audience.
Supporting material (presentation content, slides, or handouts) partially supports the ideas and minimal irrelevant content is presented. Presentation reflects a recognition of the audience but message is not fully tailored to the audience.
Insufficient supporting material (presentation content, slides, or handouts) to convey ideas or irrelevant content is presented. Message is not tailored to audience.



Central Message
Central message is compelling (precisely stated, appropriately repeated, memorable, and strongly supported.)
Central message is clear and consistent with the supporting material.
Central message is basically understandable but is not often repeated and is not memorable.
Central message can be deduced, but is not explicitly stated in the presentation.








Presentation materials rubric






Warning



PRESENTATION MATERIALS RUBRIC







Trait
Professional Quality (4)
Minor Revision Required (3)
Major Revisions Required (2)
Unacceptable or Missing (1–0)




Design: Backgrounds, Layout, Theme and Images Enhance Understanding
Design is effective and all best practices are followed. No revisions needed.
Effective design is used; only a few slides need revisions in layout, font, or visual appeal to achieve professional quality.
Effective design attempted but success varies across slides.
Distracting, unprofessional, and/or entirely unrelated to content.


Design: Use of Text is Limited and Appropriate to Complement Oral Message, Not Compete With it
Use of text is appropriately limited and effectively supports oral messages.
Use of text is generally effective throughout all slides with few minor revisions needed to achieve professional quality.
Effectiveness of text varies across slides—some may exhibit too much text or text is so limited that it is cryptic.
Excessive use of text detracts from oral presentation, text is illegible, or text is wholly unrelated to oral message.


Design: Use of Color Conveys Meaning
Color is used to convey meaning throughout and consistent across slides to enable reader to connect key points or understand similar visuals.
Color is usually used to convey meaning and is consistent across most slides and generally helps reader connect key points or understand similar visuals across slides, but some slides still exhibit minor problems.
Color is usually used to convey meaning and is consistent across most slides and generally helps reader connect key points or understand similar visuals across slides, but some slides still exhibit major problems.
Color is not used to convey meaning or is inconsistent throughout the presentation materials to the point of obscuring understanding.


Organization: Is Natural and Contributes to Central Message
Slides follow a clear organizational structure aided by headings and slide design that is natural and adds to logical and convincing support for key message.
Slides follow a clear organizational structure aided by headings and slide design but minor problems in sequencing or ineffective repetition may remain that either detract from or belabor the key message.
Organizational flow is clearly attempted but is ineffective or not consistently adhered to.
Slide order is disjointed or obviously organized around presenters rather than content.


Content: Visual Displays of Results (Graphs and Tables) are appropriate for analysis and intuitive for audience
Visual displays are appropriate for the data type and easily interpreted by a nontechnical audience and the key takeaway is clear from the visual alone.
Visual displays are appropriate for the data type but minor revisions are needed to improve comprehension for nontechnical audience or to convey key takeaway.
Visual displays may be technically correct but are very difficult for nontechnical audience to understand or attempt to convey too much information in one visual.
Improper visual displays are used for the data type or question.


Content: Visual Displays of Results are Legible
Graphs/tables and accompanying labels are all legible and all graph attributes are clearly rendered to enable comprehension.
No graphs/tables exhibit major problems described in level (1) but some may require minor revisions to improve clarity (e.g., patterns, hue or contrast, or small problems with font).
Some but not all graphs/tables exhibit major problems described in level (1).
Graphs or tables are illegible or too poorly labeled or rendered to allow for comprehension. Problems may include small font, poor color contrast, or markers/lines that are too small.


Content: Relevant and Succinct
Materials include no irrelevant content and conveys Key Takeaways and Recommendations effectively and succinctly.
Materials include minimal irrelevant content but may use repetition ineffectively or leave out some key content that would strengthen Key Takeaways and Recommendations.
Materials include some irrelevant content OR major omissions of relevant content exist but the audience can follow the Key Takeaways and Recommendations.
Materials include substantial irrelevant content or content that is obviously inappropriate for the audience (e.g., R code, detailed output from statistical tests).







Formal documentation of work






Warning



FORMAL DOCUMENTATION OF WORK


The following simple rubric will be used to assign grades for documentation of work. Please refer to any supplemental guidelines provided by your instructor.

Is documentation sufficient to follow the analysis conducted? Can a data analyst follow your process from raw data to output/conclusions?
Does code run without errors from start to finish when beginning with an empty environment?
Does code reproduce all content included in the presentation materials without major omissions?
Are analyses performed in Excel/Tableau sufficiently documented? Can a data analyst recreate your analysis with the documentation provided?
Is organization across and within files effective for matching presented work to the code that produced it?
Are there discrepancies between the actions the code performs and the way the output is presented in the slides or oral presentation? For example, does the code use filters appropriately to produce analysis for a subset of workers as reported in the slides?
Does the code contain appropriate inferential statistics to accompany descriptive analysis presented in the presentation?

title: GROUP PROJECT – IN PERSON PRESENTATION
text:
Scenario and audience






Note



SCENARIO AND AUDIENCE


Treat this as a formal business presentation to decision makers who need a clear story, relevant evidence, and practical recommendations.
Your audience may not be experts in statistics. Your goal is not to show everything you did. Your goal is to help the audience understand: - what question you investigated, - what you found, - why it matters, - and what they should do next.

text:
Delivery requirements






Note



DELIVERY REQUIREMENTS


Requirements for preparation and delivery are reflected in the rubric for the in-person presentation.






Warning



MINIMUM EXPECTATIONS



Practice together as a group.
Aim for a cohesive presentation rather than a collection of separate mini-presentations.
All group members should speak for roughly equal amounts of time.
At minimum, wear something that would be appropriate for a job interview. Business casual or professional attire are both acceptable.

title: GROUP PROJECT – IN PERSON PRESENTATION
text:
Presentation expectations






Note



PRESENTATION EXPECTATIONS


Give an 8(ish) minute presentation with additional time at the end for questions from the audience.
Because time is limited, your presentation must be clear and concise while still conveying your message fully and effectively. Do not try to show every part of your analysis. Instead, curate your results. Focus on the most important evidence needed to support your story and conclusions.
Aim to make connections between ideas and maintain smooth flow across the presentation.






Warning



WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE



Do not rush.
Do not try to include every result you produced.
Prioritize the strongest and most decision-relevant findings.
Make your key takeaways clear early, then support them with evidence.

title: GROUP PROJECT – IN PERSON PRESENTATION
text:
Visual aid requirements






Note



VISUAL AID


A visual aid is required. Create slides that are professional and that engage the interest of the audience. The slides should help the audience understand and remember your key points.






Warning



SLIDE DESIGN TIPS



Do not put everything you want to say onto the slides. The slides are not your teleprompter.
Put figures, tables, and visuals on the slide, then discuss the details aloud.
Aim for a consistent and cohesive appearance in terms of theme and color scheme.
Limit text and avoid garish colors.
Use color with purpose to direct the audience’s attention to key numbers or patterns.
If you have a visualization on a slide, make it the star of that slide. Do not clutter the slide with extra text boxes.
Consider including a “road map” slide or recurring visual cue to help the audience track your progress.
Avoid copying and pasting raw statistical output from RStudio into the slides.
Avoid pasting raw tables from RStudio into the slides. Recreate tables in slide software or Excel, or use polished outputs such as kable() in R Markdown when appropriate.
You can and should paste finished visualizations into your presentation.

title: GROUP PROJECT – IN PERSON PRESENTATION
text:
Recommended presentation structure
You may organize your presentation as you wish, but it should contain the following major elements.






Warning



INTRODUCTION



Introduce yourselves.
Explain why this analysis matters for your decision makers.
Provide enough background information to set the stage.
Do not begin by diving directly into the data.
Briefly identify the audience or decision maker your presentation is targeting.
Include a short road map or agenda.







Warning



OVERALL CONCLUSION AND CENTRAL MESSAGE


State your key takeaways early. The audience should learn your main message near the beginning of the presentation and then see the evidence that supports it.
Throughout the presentation, incorporate smooth transitions between speakers and between sections. Ideally, transitions should help reinforce the logic of your story.






Warning



VARIABLES AND APPROACH


Summarize your overall approach to the analysis.
Explain: - what variables you used, - what they measure, - any created measures or unfamiliar terms, - and how the audience should think about the analysis at a high level.
Assume the audience has not seen the data before.






Warning



KEY FINDINGS


Use your data to support your conclusions by presenting a number of relevant key findings.
For each figure or table: - explain what it shows, - explain why it matters, - and connect it to the conclusion you are drawing.
This is one of the most important parts of the presentation and should be especially well organized.






Warning



RECOMMENDATIONS / CONCLUSION


Briefly reiterate your key takeaways from the analysis.
Then make recommendation(s) based on your findings. Recommendations do not need to be technical. Instead, focus on the implications of your analysis for the decision makers.






Warning



CLOSING


End strong. Reinforce the central message, briefly restate the key takeaway, and invite questions.

title: GROUP PROJECT – IN PERSON PRESENTATION
text:
Suggested presenter checklist






Note



PRESENTER CHECKLIST







Before presenting, make sure your team can say yes to each item




We have a clear decision maker or target audience in mind.


We state our main takeaway early in the presentation.


Our slides support the story instead of repeating a script.


Our visuals are readable and easy for a nontechnical audience to understand.


We avoid raw R output and overly technical language on slides.


Each figure or table has a clear purpose and takeaway.


All group members speak and transitions feel practiced.


Our recommendations follow logically from our findings.


We can answer basic questions about how we conducted the analysis.

text:
Grading criteria






Note



GRADING CRITERIA


Delivery requirements for preparation and presentation are reflected in the rubric for the in-person presentation. Use that rubric as your guide while practicing and refining your slides.
The strongest presentations will: - communicate a clear and memorable message, - use visuals effectively, - stay audience-centered, - and connect evidence to recommendations.

title: Project 2 Rubric
text:
Criterion 1: Week 13 Informal Meeting (10 points)
Professional Quality (10-8 points)
Team arrives prepared with a real topic, a clear problem or opportunity, and a plausible research direction. Team can explain who or what might be studied and why the topic is worth pursuing.
High Quality with Minor Issues (8-5 points)
Team arrives with a workable topic, but the problem, audience, or research direction is still somewhat vague or underdeveloped.
Low Quality with Major Issues (5-1 points)
Team is underprepared. Topic is unclear, too broad, or not yet connected to a workable research design.
No Marks (0 points)
Team does not participate or does not present a meaningful topic or direction.

title: Project 2 Rubric
text:
Criterion 2: Week 14 Informal Presentation (10 points)
Professional Quality (10-8 points)
Presentation clearly explains the problem or opportunity, the research question, the proposed design, and why the design could produce trustworthy evidence. The audience can understand what is being proposed and why it matters.
High Quality with Minor Issues (8-5 points)
Presentation is understandable, but one or more elements are not clearly developed, such as the research question, the fit between question and design, or the explanation of trustworthiness.
Low Quality with Major Issues (5-1 points)
Presentation is difficult to follow, lacks important components, or does not make a convincing case for the design.
No Marks (0 points)
Presentation is missing or does not meaningfully address the assignment.

title: Project 2 Rubric
section: Criterion 3: Week 14 Red Team Critique (10 points)
text:
Criterion 3: Week 14 Red Team Critique (10 points)
Professional Quality (10-8 points)
Critique is serious, professional, and useful. Team identifies meaningful risks or weaknesses related to sampling, measurement, design, ethics, generalization, or limitations and offers feedback that could genuinely improve the project.
High Quality with Minor Issues (8-5 points)
Critique identifies some real concerns, but the feedback is somewhat general, incomplete, or not fully developed.
Low Quality with Major Issues (5-1 points)
Critique is superficial, unfocused, or too vague to help improve the proposal.
No Marks (0 points)
Critique is missing or does not meaningfully engage with another team’s proposal.

title: Project 2 Rubric
section: Criterion 4: Written Proposal - Problem / Opportunity (15 points)
text:
Criterion 4: Written Proposal - Problem / Opportunity (15 points)
Professional Quality (15-12 points)
Written report clearly identifies the decision maker, stakeholder, or audience and clearly explains the problem or opportunity. It is easy to see why the question matters and how the results could inform a real decision.
High Quality with Minor Issues (12-8 points)
Problem or opportunity is present but not fully clear, specific, or well connected to decision-making.
Low Quality with Major Issues (8-1 points)
Section is vague, thin, or underdeveloped. The reader cannot clearly tell what problem is being addressed or why it matters.
No Marks (0 points)
Section is missing or not meaningfully addressed.

title: Project 2 Rubric
section: Criterion 5: Written Proposal - Research Question and Direction (15 points)
text:
Criterion 5: Written Proposal - Research Question and Direction (15 points)
Professional Quality (15-12 points)
Written report states a specific, interesting, and actionable research question. The scope is focused enough to study, and any supporting objectives or hypotheses help clarify the design rather than distract from it.
High Quality with Minor Issues (12-8 points)
Research question is workable but somewhat broad, narrow, or loosely connected to the proposed design.
Low Quality with Major Issues (8-1 points)
Research question is unclear, unfocused, or not actionable.
No Marks (0 points)
Section is missing or not meaningfully addressed.

title: Project 2 Rubric
section: Criterion 6: Written Proposal - Study Design and Measures (20 points)
text:
Criterion 6: Written Proposal - Study Design and Measures (20 points)
Professional Quality (20-16 points)
Written report clearly explains the proposed method, defines who or what will be studied, and describes what information would be collected and how. The design is concrete enough that a reader can imagine how the study would actually be carried out.
High Quality with Minor Issues (16-10 points)
Study design is reasonable, but parts of the method, measurement plan, or data collection process remain unclear or underdeveloped.
Low Quality with Major Issues (10-1 points)
Study design is vague, incomplete, or not clearly connected to the research question.
No Marks (0 points)
Section is missing or not meaningfully addressed.

title: Project 2 Rubric
section: Criterion 7: Written Proposal - Trustworthiness, Risks, and Limits (20 points)
text:
Criterion 7: Written Proposal - Trustworthiness, Risks, and Limits (20 points)
Professional Quality (20-16 points)
Written report thoughtfully addresses sampling, representation, measurement, bias, limitations, and ethics. It shows real reflection about what the study could support, what could go wrong, and why the evidence might still be worth using.
High Quality with Minor Issues (16-10 points)
Report addresses trustworthiness and limitations, but some important risks, assumptions, or ethical concerns are only briefly discussed.
Low Quality with Major Issues (10-1 points)
Discussion of trustworthiness, bias, limitations, or ethics is thin, generic, or incomplete.
No Marks (0 points)
Section is missing or not meaningfully addressed.

text:
This prompt is for the Practicum portion of your final exam. Please review it carefully before you arrive for the exam. The scenario and data description are included here. You will receive the actual data at the start of the exam period. This exercise is open note, book, Google etc., but is not a team exercise. You must complete your work without communicating with others. However, you are welcome to discuss the prompt and your strategy with others before class. The rubric does include points for originality of work.






NoteScenario



The Pension Benefit Guarantee Corporation (PBGC) is a governmental agency that pays pension benefits to workers when their pension plans become insolvent. So, if a pension plan is unable to pay benefits to retirees, the PBGC will cover the liabilities up to a maximum payout of $69,750 annually per retiree. Like other insurers, the PBGC charges premiums and those funds are used to finance the payouts for any plans that become insolvent. Any employer with a pension fund covered by the PBGC must pay premiums.
The PBGC must closely track payouts to ensure it is collecting enough money to cover liabilities. Your consulting firm has been tasked with analyzing PBGC payouts to insolvent funds between fiscal years 2005 and 2019. Your team has decided to address the following questions in their report:

Are plans equally distributed across states or do some states have more insolvent plans than others?
Is the average payment amount increasing over time?
In 2019, was the average payment per participant lower than the maximum benefit of $69,750?









NoteData Description



The data grouping is panel, but payment and participant information is missing in years when the plan did not receive any payment. These rows have already been excluded from the data for you. You will not need to remove missing data before conducting your analysis.
The unit of analysis is one observation per plan per year. Plans that the PBGC provided payments for over multiple years will appear in multiple rows.
The variables are:

PIN: Plan identification number
PlanName: Name of the plan (e.g. “ALA Lithographic Industry Pension Plan”)
State: Two letter state abbreviation
Participants: Number of plan participants (employees who have retirement benefits through that plan)
Payment: Total payments in dollars the PBGC made to all plan participants
Year: The fiscal year when the payments occurred









NoteRequirements



Using Posit.cloud, Excel, and Tableau (optional), please conduct preliminary analysis of any of the questions above. Your analysis should include:

At least one graph
At least one table
At least one hypothesis test
A brief bullet point summary of your findings

You do not need to address all questions! You may choose to focus on only one or just a few.

text:

Week 6 & 7 resources and lectures
Your lecture examples for idt(), idw(), pst(), psw(), and ost()









ImportantInstructions




Load the dataset into R as df


df <- read.csv('../shared/data/airbnb_chicago.csv')


Review the full example in Hypothesis 1.
Complete steps 4–5 for Hypothesis 2.
Attempt your own full test for Hypothesis 3 using one of the following: idt(), idw(), pst(), psw(), or ost().
For step 5, include both the practical meaning of the result and whether the effect size suggests the result is small, medium, or large.
If your code will not knit, leave your attempted code in the chunk and comment out lines with #.







What statistical story am I attempting to tell?

Properties that are instantly bookable will have a lower mean price than those that are not.

What have I estimated or plotted to go along with that story and what is my conclusion from those estimates alone? If there was no uncertainty in these estimates, what should the business do?




Average List Price by Instant Bookable


Properties that are instantly bookable appear to have a lower mean price than those that are not.

Which test is appropriate and what is the null hypothesis?

Test Type: Independent Samples t-Test idt()
\(H_0\): \(\mu_{\text{Instant Bookable}} = \mu_{\text{Not Instant Bookable}}\)
\(H_A\): \(\mu_{\text{Instant Bookable}} \neq \mu_{\text{Not Instant Bookable}}\)
\(\alpha = 0.05\)

h1 <- df %>%
  idt(listed_price ~ instant_bookable)

[1] "Independent variable converted to a factor using as.factor()"

print(h1)

$analysis_type
[1] "Independent t-Test, Two Tailed test"

$results
[1] "t(2110.38) = 3.515, p = 0, r = 0.076, bf10 = 12.163"

$descriptive_statistics
  Group       N    Mean Standard_Error
1     f 2660.00  137.00           2.47
2     t 1060.00  122.00           3.59



Statistical Interpretation

t(2110.38) = 3.515, p = 0, r = 0.076, bf10 = 12.163
p is less than 0.05 so we reject the null hypothesis. Properties that are instantly bookable have a statistically significant difference in mean listed price compared to those that are not instantly bookable.

Practical Interpretation

There is evidence that instantly bookable properties are priced differently from properties that are not instantly bookable. In this sample, instantly bookable properties have a lower average listed price. One possible explanation is that owners may use instant booking to attract more customers when their property is in a more competitive market or lower-demand area.
Cohen’s \(d\) is small, which suggests that booking policy explains only a small portion of the overall variation in listed price. Bayes factor indicates strong evidence that this difference is real, but the effect size suggests that booking policy alone is not one of the most important drivers of price. In business terms, instant booking may matter, but owners would still need to consider other larger influences such as location, property size, and amenities.





Statistical Story

Properties that are instantly bookable will have a lower median price than those that are not.

Estimates / Plot




Box Plot by Instant Bookable


Properties that are instantly bookable appear to have a lower median listed price than those that are not. The distribution of listed price is highly skewed, so the median may describe the center better than the mean.

Test and Hypothesis

Test Type: Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Independent Samples) idw()
\(H_0\): \(\text{Median}_{\text{Instant Bookable}} = \text{Median}_{\text{Not Instant Bookable}}\)
\(H_A\): \(\text{Median}_{\text{Instant Bookable}} \neq \text{Median}_{\text{Not Instant Bookable}}\)
\(\alpha = 0.05\)

h2 <- df %>%
  idw(listed_price ~ instant_bookable)

[1] "Independent variable converted to a factor using as.factor()"

print(h2)

$analysis_type
[1] "Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Independent Samples), Two Tailed test"

$results
[1] "W = 1590257, p = 0, r = 0.101"

$descriptive_statistics
  Group    N Median
1     f 2660    100
2     t 1060     88



Statistical Interpretation

W = 1590257, p = 0, r = 0.101

Practical Interpretation

title: What Is Data Literacy?
What Is Data Literacy?
What Is Data Literacy?
text:
Data literacy in the workplace
Effective analysts combine three kinds of knowledge:

subject-matter knowledge to ask useful questions and recognize implausible results;
statistical and technical skills to prepare, summarize, visualize, and analyze data; and
communication skills to explain what the evidence means for a decision.

Data literacy also requires technological agility. Specific software will change, but the ability to inspect unfamiliar data, learn a new tool, verify results, and communicate limitations remains valuable across industries.

title: What Is Data Literacy?
text:
Scope of this course
The course emphasizes descriptive and introductory inferential analysis using structured data. Later weeks introduce survey research, experimental design, and machine learning, but the central goal remains sound reasoning: understand the row, ask a defensible question, use an appropriate method, and communicate what the evidence does and does not support.

text:
Observations and variables

An observation is one row.
A variable is one column that records an attribute or measurement.
An identifier distinguishes entities but is not automatically a quantity worth averaging.









Variable

Compare distributions; interpret using its documented scale

An all-numeric column is not necessarily quantitative. ZIP codes, product codes, and patient IDs are labels even when stored as numbers.

title: Understanding Data
text:
Data structure changes the question

Cross-sectional data
A cross-section compares many entities at one point or period in time. For example, a single Airbnb snapshot can compare listings across neighborhoods.


Time-series data
A time series follows one measure for one entity or aggregate over time. Daily average sleep duration for the entire sample is a time series.


Panel data
Panel data follows multiple entities over time. The main-sleep records form a panel because the same people appear on many dates.

main_sleep <- sleep[sleep$SleepEventType == "Main", ]
person_days <- aggregate(Date ~ PersonName, main_sleep, function(x) length(unique(x)))
names(person_days)[2] <- "RecordedDays"
knitr::kable(person_days, caption = "Repeated observations make this a panel data set")

section: Wide and long are descriptions, not judgments
text:
Wide and long are descriptions, not judgments
The sleep-stage columns (REMMinutes, DeepMinutes, and LightMinutes) are stored wide: each stage has its own column. The same information could be made long with one Stage column and one Minutes column.
Wide data can be convenient for a report. Long data is often easier for grouped summaries and graphs. Choose the structure that supports the analysis, while keeping the grain explicit.

title: Measures of Variability
text:
Range
The range is the distance from the smallest observation to the largest:
[ = - ]

diff(range(x))

[1] 218


The range is easy to explain, but it uses only two observations. A single unusual value can change it dramatically.

title: Measures of Variability
text:
Interquartile range
The interquartile range (IQR) describes the width of the middle 50% of observations:
[ = Q_3 - Q_1 ]

quantile(x, c(.25, .50, .75))

25% 50% 75% 
428 453 476 

IQR(x)

[1] 48


Because it focuses on the middle half, the IQR is more resistant to unusually high or low values than the range. It is a natural companion to the median and the box plot.

title: Measures of Variability
text:
Standard deviation
Standard deviation describes typical distance from the mean. Larger values indicate more spread around the mean.

mean(x)

[1] 450.5912

sd(x)

[1] 37.12756


R’s sd() calculates the sample standard deviation, using (n-1) in the denominator. If the observations are the entire population of interest rather than a sample, the population calculation is:

population_sd <- sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))
population_sd

[1] 37.11046


Always state which population you want to describe. A complete course data file is not automatically the complete real-world population.

title: Measures of Variability
text:
What an outlier changes
The next comparison adds one implausible 1,200-minute sleep record to illustrate sensitivity. This is a diagnostic example, not a recommendation to delete high values.

x_with_outlier <- c(x, 1200)

outlier_comparison <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Mean", "Median", "Range", "IQR", "Sample SD"),
  Original = c(mean(x), median(x), diff(range(x)), IQR(x), sd(x)),
  WithOutlier = c(mean(x_with_outlier), median(x_with_outlier),
                  diff(range(x_with_outlier)), IQR(x_with_outlier),

)

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
A strong interpretation connects visible evidence to the question being asked without claiming more than the data can support.
Use this sequence:

Observation: What pattern, comparison, or unusual feature is visible?
Evidence: Which values, groups, or time periods support the observation?
Explanation: What plausible mechanisms could produce it?
Limitation: What else could explain it, and what can the graph not establish?
Implication: What decision or next analysis does the result support?

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
A strong interpretation connects visible evidence to the question being asked without claiming more than the data can support.
Use this sequence:

Observation: What pattern, comparison, or unusual feature is visible?
Evidence: Which values, groups, or time periods support the observation?
Explanation: What plausible mechanisms could produce it?
Limitation: What else could explain it, and what can the graph not establish?
Implication: What decision or next analysis does the result support?

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
Example 1: a distribution





Distribution of main-sleep duration in the course data




Weak: Most people sleep around the average.
Stronger: Main-sleep duration is concentrated in the middle of the observed range, with fewer records at both extremes. Before using the mean as the only summary, compare it with the median and inspect the unusual low and high values. The graph describes recorded sleep events in this sample; it does not establish how much sleep people need.
The stronger version identifies the shape, names a useful follow-up, and limits the population claim.

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
Example 2: group comparisons





Listed price by room type, excluding values above $500 so the central distributions remain visible




Observation: The price distributions differ by room type, and each group contains substantial variation.
Evidence: Compare medians, IQRs, and the degree of overlap rather than focusing only on the most expensive listing.
Limitation: Room type is not the only difference among listings. Neighborhood, capacity, amenities, review history, and timing may all be related to price. Filtering at $500 improves readability but means the graph does not display the full upper tail.
Implication: Room type is a useful starting segmentation variable, but a pricing recommendation should examine additional variables and the unfiltered data.

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
Interpret the visual encoding too
Before interpreting the subject matter, check how the graph was built.







Check
Why it matters




Axis limits and transformations
Truncation or a log scale changes visual distance


Counts versus percentages
Different denominators can reverse a comparison


Aggregation
A monthly average can hide daily variation


Filters and exclusions
The displayed population may be narrower than the title suggests


Color and size
Encodings may imply importance or magnitude


Missing values
Unshown observations may not be missing at random


Sample size
A dramatic pattern based on a few records may be unstable

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
Avoid common overclaims







Avoid
Prefer




“X causes Y” from an observational graph
“X and Y are associated in these data”


“The groups are significantly different” from visual separation
“The displayed distributions differ; a formal test is needed for statistical significance”


“Most customers prefer…” without a denominator
“Among the respondents shown, X of N (Y%) selected…”


“Sales increased because of the campaign”
“Sales increased after the campaign; seasonality and other changes remain possible explanations”


“There is no relationship”
“No clear relationship is visible at this scale”

title: Interpreting Data Visualizations
text:
A reusable interpretation paragraph

The graph shows [pattern] for [population and period]. The clearest evidence is [specific comparison or value]. One plausible explanation is [mechanism], although [alternative explanation or data limitation] means the graph does not establish [unsupported claim]. The result suggests [decision or next analysis].







TipRead the title last



First inspect the axes, units, legend, filters, and source. Then read the title and decide whether its claim matches the evidence actually displayed.

title: Analysis Plan Outline
text:
An analysis plan connects a decision problem to the data, methods, and communication needed to answer it. Writing the plan first exposes missing variables, ambiguous definitions, and unrealistic claims before they become expensive.
This page is a planning aid. The Project 1 prompt and Project 1 timeline remain the authoritative sources for required deliverables and dates.

title: Analysis Plan Outline
text:
An analysis plan connects a decision problem to the data, methods, and communication needed to answer it. Writing the plan first exposes missing variables, ambiguous definitions, and unrealistic claims before they become expensive.
This page is a planning aid. The Project 1 prompt and Project 1 timeline remain the authoritative sources for required deliverables and dates.

title: Analysis Plan Outline
text:
1. Decision context
State:

the stakeholder or audience;
the decision, action, or opportunity;
why the decision matters; and
what is outside the stakeholder’s control.

Template: [Stakeholder] needs to decide [decision] because [business consequence].

title: Analysis Plan Outline
text:
2. Research question
Write one focused question that names the outcome, population, time, and important comparison.
Template: Among [population] during [period], how does [outcome] vary with or across [explanatory variables/groups], for the purpose of [decision]?
Avoid a question that assumes its conclusion or requires data you do not have.

title: Analysis Plan Outline
text:
3. Objectives
List concrete analytical products. Useful verbs include describe, compare, estimate, identify, assess, rank, forecast, and recommend.
Example:

Describe monthly crash volume and severity.
Compare severe-outcome percentages across selected conditions.
Identify geographic and temporal segments for deeper review.
Recommend a limited next step supported by the evidence.

Each objective should help answer the research question. Remove interesting side analyses that do not.

title: Analysis Plan Outline
text:
4. Data and grain
For every input table, record:



Planning item
What to write




Source
Publisher, file or URL, snapshot/version


Grain
What one row represents


Coverage
Population, geography, and period


Join keys
Exact fields and expected relationship


Outcome
Variable and operational definition


Explanatory variables
Fields used for grouping or modeling


Missingness
Important unavailable or incomplete fields


Ethics/privacy
Risks, restrictions, and necessary exclusions









WarningCheck joins before analysis



State whether each join should be one-to-one, many-to-one, or one-to-many. Compare row counts and key uniqueness before and after joining. Unexpected row multiplication can invalidate every result.

title: ECO 230 Business and Economic Research & Communication
text:
Course description
Building on the foundation in statistics acquired in STAT 145, students will continue to develop and will apply skills in data analysis to aid in business decision making. These skills include data collection, data summarization, data visualization, statistical inference, and communication of data in business contexts. Calculation of individual grades for team project work
All work for the assignments denoted as Team Projects by (T) above will be scored out of 100 points to assign a Team Grade. Individual grades will be computed by multiplying the Team Grade by the CATME peer evaluation score you receive for that work. The CATME peer evaluation is a psychometrically validated and behaviorally anchored rating scale developed under a National Science Foundation Grant and used by universities throughout the country. Through a secure web-based platform, you will rate your own and your teammate’s performance on each project. This information will be reported in the aggregate to your teammates (they cannot see who gave them what scores) and will produce a Peer Evaluation Score. Most students receive a score of 1, those that exhibit exceptional performance receive scores above 1 with a maximum of 1.05. Underperforming teammates receive scores below 1, and as low as 0.4.






Note



Note: This is not a “zero sum game”. It is possible for team members to get scores above 1 without others getting scores below. The algorithm flags evaluations that appear to manipulate ratings to inflate their own scores. Your score will automatically be reduced by 0.05 if you fail to complete the Peer Evaluation on or before the due date.




Grievance procedure for peer evaluation scores
Poor peer evaluations can lead an individual grade to fall substantially below the Team Grade. For example, a project that received a score of 95/100 would produce an individual grade of 38/100 if you receive a peer evaluation score of 0.4. If you feel the score you received does not accurately reflect your contributions to Team Project work, you have the option to file a grievance. To do so you must follow this procedure:

Within 2 business days of the official notification that grades have been posted, communicate to your instructor via email your intent to file a grievance. Official notifications of grade posting will appear on Canvas notifications.
Within 1 business day of notifying your intent, prepare and email a one page formal letter addressed to your teammates and including the following information:

Your understanding of the work you had agreed to do for the deliverable. Be sure to refer to any documentation that is relevant (Meeting Minutes, emails or group chats, revision histories in documents etc.). Be prepared to provide any documentation you mention in the letter if requested.
A summary of the work you actually did. Refer to documentation as above.
Justification for any discrepancies between (a) and (b). If this documentation includes any confidential health or personal matters you do not wish to disclose to your team, please raise this with me or contact Student Life Office for council. Note: In these cases it is best to reach out to me or Student Life before you are at the point of receiving a bad peer evaluation.
A statement of the peer evaluation score you believe you have earned.

If after reviewing your letter I believe the case has merit, I will send it on to your teammates and schedule an arbitration. If I determine no arbitration is warranted, I will schedule a one-on-one meeting with you to discuss.
If arbitration is warranted, it must be conducted in-person with all team members present. The only exception to this requirement would be a case where the timeline in the procedure would place the earliest possible arbitration date after the final exam date. In those cases, a virtual meeting may be agreed upon or incomplete grades may be assigned until an in-person meeting can be scheduled. I will serve as the arbitrator. You and your teammates will have the opportunity to present your case and reconcile evidence referenced in your letter. At the end of the meeting, all team members (including yourself) will submit the score they believe you have earned to me via secret ballot. I will use this information in making my final determination, but the final determination is mine alone.

Individual assignments






Warning

When conflicts are known ahead of the deadline you must notify me ahead of the deadline. All communication regarding missed or late individual work should be confirmed by email - even if we speak in person or during student hours, you must follow up via email to confirm so that we both have a record of the agreement.

Deadlines for Team Assignments may be extended for the entire class if there are extenuating circumstances or granted to teams if requested with appropriate justification and all team members agree to the request. Presentations cannot be delayed unless there is a major emergency or complication. For other deliverables, extensions must be requested at least 1 business day before the due date. Be prepared to show appropriate documentation of work to date and to provide an explanation for the value you will add to the final product if the extension is granted. Unless a request is made and granted, late assignments will receive a grade of 0.

Quizzes may be rescheduled only in the case of serious illness, injury, or significant academic or professional development opportunity. Although attendance will not be formally recorded for all class meetings, your Team can and should reduce your peer evaluation score if you miss meetings or are absent during in class Work Days. To avoid this consequence, you should:

Communicate clearly with your team any time you will be absent from a Team Meeting or class on a day that includes Case Work Time.

Document that communication (e.g. save emails or post to team message board).

Participate actively in scheduling Team Meetings outside of class.

Lay out policies on scheduling team meetings and missed meetings and follow them.

Respect others’ time and reserve absences for only when absolutely unavoidable.

Communicate with me (your instructor) or the Office of Student Life if any situation arises that will dramatically impact your attendance in class and at team meetings (e.g. serious illness, injury or personal emergency).

title: ECO 230 Business and Economic Research & Communication
text:
Course description
Building on the foundation in statistics acquired in STAT 145, students will continue to develop and will apply skills in data analysis to aid in business decision making. These skills include data collection, data summarization, data visualization, statistical inference, and communication of data in business contexts. Students will learn and apply best practices for research design and analysis to address authentic business cases. Students will build these skills in collaboration with each other and through engagement with business and community leaders. The course also discusses effective survey design and current privacy and ethical issues in collecting and using data. Prerequisite: ENG 110 or ENG 112; STAT 145; CBA major, CASSH economics major, or healthcare analytics management minor. Offered Fall, Spring.

Prerequisites
Prerequisite: ENG 110 or ENG 112; STAT 145; CBA major, CLS economics major, or Healthcare Analytics Management Minor.

title: ECO 230 Business and Economic Research & Communication
text:

Mapped to CBA Undergraduate Curriculum Goals and Objectives

Develop the ability to articulate a business problem or opportunity using qualitative and quantitative evidence and propose an analysis plan to identify potential solutions, including collection of primary data via surveys. (CT-1)
Describe, summarize, and interpret data using descriptive statistics, inferential statistics, and data visualization.
Develop foundational skills related to spreadsheets, interactive data visualization software, and scripting languages used for data analysis and visualization.
Communicate the purpose, methods, and results of analysis to authentic audiences in appropriate written and oral formats. (CS-1, CS-2)
Apply research design and data analysis best practices to complete case-based projects and to critique others’ analyses. (CT-1)
Describe current debates in research ethics and data privacy and the implications for business research. (SR-1)

Calculations
Your overall grade consists of the following assessments, arranged by type and value. Your final grade can be computed by multiplying the scores received by the percentages reported below to arrive at a weighted average. Team assignments are denoted by (T) but please note grades received for team project deliverables will be adjusted by your Peer Evaluation score.

Calculation of individual grades for team project work
All work for the assignments denoted as Team Projects by (T) above will be scored out of 100 points to assign a Team Grade. Individual grades will be computed by multiplying the Team Grade by the CATME peer evaluation score you receive for that work. The CATME peer evaluation is a psychometrically validated and behaviorally anchored rating scale developed under a National Science Foundation Grant and used by universities throughout the country. Through a secure web-based platform, you will rate your own and your teammate’s performance on each project. This information will be reported in the aggregate to your teammates (they cannot see who gave them what scores) and will produce a Peer Evaluation Score. Most students receive a score of 1, those that exhibit exceptional performance receive scores above 1 with a maximum of 1.05. Underperforming teammates receive scores below 1, and as low as 0.4.






Note



Note: This is not a “zero sum game”. It is possible for team members to get scores above 1 without others getting scores below. The algorithm flags evaluations that appear to manipulate ratings to inflate their own scores. Your score will automatically be reduced by 0.05 if you fail to complete the Peer Evaluation on or before the due date.




Grievance procedure for peer evaluation scores
Poor peer evaluations can lead an individual grade to fall substantially below the Team Grade. For example, a project that received a score of 95/100 would produce an individual grade of 38/100 if you receive a peer evaluation score of 0.4. If you feel the score you received does not accurately reflect your contributions to Team Project work, you have the option to file a grievance. To do so you must follow this procedure:

Within 2 business days of the official notification that grades have been posted, communicate to your instructor via email your intent to file a grievance. Official notifications of grade posting will appear on Canvas notifications.
Within 1 business day of notifying your intent, prepare and email a one page formal letter addressed to your teammates and including the following information:

Your understanding of the work you had agreed to do for the deliverable. Be sure to refer to any documentation that is relevant (Meeting Minutes, emails or group chats, revision histories in documents etc.). Be prepared to provide any documentation you mention in the letter if requested.
A summary of the work you actually did. Refer to documentation as above.
Justification for any discrepancies between (a) and (b). If this documentation includes any confidential health or personal matters you do not wish to disclose to your team, please raise this with me or contact Student Life Office for council. Note: In these cases it is best to reach out to me or Student Life before you are at the point of receiving a bad peer evaluation.
A statement of the peer evaluation score you believe you have earned.

If after reviewing your letter I believe the case has merit, I will send it on to your teammates and schedule an arbitration. If I determine no arbitration is warranted, I will schedule a one-on-one meeting with you to discuss.
If arbitration is warranted, it must be conducted in-person with all team members present. The only exception to this requirement would be a case where the timeline in the procedure would place the earliest possible arbitration date after the final exam date. In those cases, a virtual meeting may be agreed upon or incomplete grades may be assigned until an in-person meeting can be scheduled. I will serve as the arbitrator. You and your teammates will have the opportunity to present your case and reconcile evidence referenced in your letter. At the end of the meeting, all team members (including yourself) will submit the score they believe you have earned to me via secret ballot. I will use this information in making my final determination, but the final determination is mine alone.

Individual assignments






Warning



Individual assignments are due on the dates indicated on the Canvas Weekly Agendas. Late or missing assignments will not be graded. All assignments in a module must be completed before the Module Quiz. If extenuating circumstances impact your ability to meet deadlines or participate in class activities, you are responsible for alerting me as soon as possible. When conflicts are known ahead of the deadline you must notify me ahead of the deadline. All communication regarding missed or late individual work should be confirmed by email - even if we speak in person or during student hours, you must follow up via email to confirm so that we both have a record of the agreement.




Team assignments
Deadlines for Team Assignments may be extended for the entire class if there are extenuating circumstances or granted to teams if requested with appropriate justification and all team members agree to the request. Presentations cannot be delayed unless there is a major emergency or complication. For other deliverables, extensions must be requested at least 1 business day before the due date. Be prepared to show appropriate documentation of work to date and to provide an explanation for the value you will add to the final product if the extension is granted. Unless a request is made and granted, late assignments will receive a grade of 0.


Missed quizzes
Quizzes may be rescheduled only in the case of serious illness, injury, or significant academic or professional development opportunity. Personal travel or family vacations will not be accommodated unless they are associated with a significant life event (birth, death, marriage, graduation). In all cases, documentation is required. Contact me via email as soon as you know you have a conflict. Local or phone/Skype job interviews are not considered significant professional development opportunities.



Attendance and participation
Although attendance will not be formally recorded for all class meetings, your Team can and should reduce your peer evaluation score if you miss meetings or are absent during in class Work Days. To avoid this consequence, you should:

Communicate clearly with your team any time you will be absent from a Team Meeting or class on a day that includes Case Work Time.

Document that communication (e.g. save emails or post to team message board).

Participate actively in scheduling Team Meetings outside of class.

Lay out policies on scheduling team meetings and missed meetings and follow them.
